question: Can language-model training data be represented as interdependent skills, and can a learned directed skill graph drive a token-efficient mixture that adapts as those skills are learned?

key_findings.claim: The paper operationalizes a skill through held-out loss improvement and an ordered skill set through data-efficient directed transfer, making the usefulness of a proposed grouping empirically falsifiable.
key_findings.evidence: An edge from skill i to skill j exists when training on a fixed-budget mixture of their data reaches a target loss on j with no more data than training on j alone. The resulting graphs distinguish unhelpful near-complete Alpaca instruction-type groupings (97.4% dense), near-empty Pile of Law source groupings (3.9% dense), and an intermediate Natural Instructions task-category graph (42.7% dense).

anchors.section: 2.1 Complete, empty, and intermediate skill graphs

key_findings.claim: SKILL-IT converts a fixed directed skill graph and live per-skill validation losses into a dynamic multiplicative-weights data mixture.
key_findings.evidence: The paper assumes each evaluation loss contracts according to the mixture-weighted incoming graph edges, derives an online mirror-descent update, and upweights training skills that influence high-loss evaluation skills. Brute-force graph learning costs O(Hk^2); a linear O(hk) approximation trains once per source skill and measures cross-skill loss change.

key_findings.claim: Skill-aware sampling produces large gains on deliberately structured synthetic tasks and smaller but recurring improvements on Natural Instructions, including transfer from a 125M graph to a 1.3B model.
key_findings.evidence: On five-skill LEGO continual pretraining, SKILL-IT reaches 99.4% average exact classification accuracy versus 98.5% for skill-stratified sampling and 62.9% for random sampling. In fine-tuning it reaches loss 0.01 in 38.1% fewer LEGO steps and 59% fewer addition steps than target-only training, and reduces Spanish question-generation and stance-detection losses by 5.3% and 13.6%. On Natural Instructions continual pretraining the average loss is 2.103 versus 2.173 for random; with the 1.3B model it is 1.883 versus 1.985 for random and 1.907 for stratified sampling.

key_findings.claim: The headline RedPajama token-efficiency result is directionally positive but too small and confounded by mixture-search cost to establish a robust threefold training-efficiency gain.
key_findings.evidence: The 3B-parameter case uses a static T=1 mixture, after graph learning trains for one billion tokens on each of seven sources. Its average evaluation-harness accuracy is 64.4 at 1B, 2B, and 3B additional tokens, versus uniform 64.2, 64.3, and 64.3; at 1B SKILL-IT wins four of eight listed tasks and loses four. The table provides no uncertainty for this scale. Thus the statement that 1B SKILL-IT exceeds 3B uniform is literally supported (64.4 versus 64.3) but not an end-to-end compute or statistically demonstrated 3x efficiency result.

method.core_idea: Partition data into behavior-linked skills, estimate a directed graph of which training skills accelerate which evaluation skills under a fixed budget, then allocate training tokens according to both graph influence and current validation loss.
method.mechanism: Graph learning estimates positive cross-skill loss reduction by short training runs or pairwise fixed-budget comparisons. Skill-stratified sampling uniformly covers graph-relevant skills. SKILL-IT initializes from incoming graph strength and repeatedly applies an exponentiated online mirror-descent update using a moving window of evaluation losses, then samples the next round's data from the normalized weights.
assumptions: Each skill has an identifiable support slice and enough held-out examples for reliable loss measurement.
Short-run directed loss transfer estimates remain useful later in training and, when reused, across model scales.
Training on a source skill monotonically contracts the losses of graph-linked evaluation skills approximately according to the proposed multiplicative dynamics.
The fixed token budget excludes neither the cost of graph estimation nor repeated evaluation unless those costs are accounted for separately.
Skill categories are externally given for most real-data experiments; unsupervised skill discovery is not assumed solved.

techniques.role: Defines a directed edge through measured fixed-budget data efficiency instead of semantic similarity alone.
Estimates edge weights from pairwise or one-source short training runs and held-out loss changes.
Removes irrelevant skills and balances the target and prerequisite skill supports.
Dynamically reallocates tokens toward sources connected to evaluation skills that remain high-loss.
Learns the graph with a 125M model and reuses it to select data for a 1.3B model.
Clusters examples by loss trajectories across multiple random training runs as a preliminary unsupervised skill-discovery method.

evaluations.setting: Five-skill LEGO continual pretraining with GPT-Neo 125M, an imbalanced 1:1:1:3:5 training distribution, 6,000 steps, and five seeds.
evaluations.metric: Per-skill validation loss and binary exact-match accuracy.
evaluations.result: SKILL-IT obtains 99.4% average accuracy and 0.012 average loss.
evaluations.baseline: Random 62.9%/0.541, curriculum 63.6%/0.535, skill-stratified 98.5%/0.046, and skill curricula.

evaluations.setting: LEGO, three-digit addition, Spanish question generation, and stance detection target-skill fine-tuning.
evaluations.metric: Steps to loss 0.01 on synthetics and final target validation loss on Natural Instructions.
evaluations.result: SKILL-IT needs 38.1% fewer LEGO steps and 59% fewer addition steps than target-only training, and lowers the two Natural Instructions losses by 5.3% and 13.6%.
evaluations.baseline: Training only on the target skill and static skill-stratified target-plus-prerequisite sampling.

evaluations.setting: Natural Instructions continual pretraining and disjoint train/test skill categories.
evaluations.metric: Average cross-entropy validation loss per skill after 5,000 steps.
evaluations.result: Continual-pretraining loss is 2.103 versus random 2.173; out-of-domain loss is 2.540 versus random 2.546 and stratified 2.572, with the lowest category loss on 11 of 12 tasks.
evaluations.baseline: Random, sample curriculum/anticurriculum, skill curricula, skill-stratified, no-graph, and static-mixture variants.

evaluations.setting: A one-trillion-token 3B model continually pretrained on seven RedPajama sources using a static graph-based mixture.
evaluations.metric: Average accuracy over eight LM Evaluation Harness tasks after 1B, 2B, and 3B additional tokens.
evaluations.result: SKILL-IT reports 64.4 at all checkpoints; uniform reports 64.2, 64.3, and 64.3.
evaluations.baseline: Uniform sampling over data sources, excluding the seven one-billion-token source-specific graph-learning runs from the headline token comparison.

evaluations.setting: Unsupervised recovery of five LEGO skills from 500 validation examples.
evaluations.result: Clustering 1,200-dimensional loss trajectories reaches 61.0% +/- 1.6%, compared with 38.4% +/- 0.8% for the best tested embedding method.
evaluations.baseline: Pretrained/trained token embeddings and Sentence-BERT embeddings.

limitations: Author-stated/in-design: most experiments assume skills are supplied as task categories, languages, reasoning depths, digits, or data sources; the unsupervised LEGO recovery reaches only 61% accuracy.

Author-stated: brute-force graph learning scales quadratically in the number of skills, while the linear approximation changes the edge definition and still requires one training run per source skill.
Reviewer inference: short-run positive loss change is noisy, asymmetric, model-state dependent, and need not encode a stable prerequisite relation or causal semantic hierarchy.
Reviewer inference: many results use toy 125M/1.3B models, small validation sets (often 50-100 examples per skill), and hand-designed synthetic skill structure.
Reviewer inference: the only 3B-scale result is a static mixture with a 0.1-0.2 average-accuracy-point advantage and does not include graph-search compute or uncertainty.
Reviewer inference: several purportedly online experiments use T=1, so they test graph-based static mixing rather than the dynamic update.
failure_modes: A dense graph collapses SKILL-IT toward stratified sampling, while an empty graph collapses it toward loss-proportional sampling, leaving little benefit over simpler methods.
Misclassified or overlapping skills cause examples and losses to be assigned to the wrong mixture component.
Negative transfer and forgetting are thresholded away when only positive edges are retained, even though they can determine an optimal schedule.
A graph learned early or on a proxy model can become stale as the target model changes representation, scale, or competence.
Loss magnitudes with different calibration or irreducible entropy can make the exponentiated update oversample intrinsically hard skills.
The graph-probing budget can exceed the data savings when there are many skills or large proxy runs.
reusable_insights: Treat a proposed data taxonomy as useful only if it predicts measurable transfer under a fixed budget; semantic diversity alone is insufficient.
Separate identifying relevant data groups from scheduling them: a static graph and a state-dependent controller solve different problems and should be ablated independently.
Report mixture-search, proxy-training, and validation overhead alongside target-training tokens when claiming end-to-end efficiency.
Use per-group training trajectories as behavioral fingerprints for discovering latent groups, but validate stability and causal transfer before calling them skills.
Test graph portability across scale, architecture, training phase, and random seed rather than assuming small-model preferences extrapolate.
open_questions: Can skills and directed transfer edges be recovered jointly from raw corpora without labels, repeated full training runs, or a fixed number of clusters?
How stable are graph direction, edge weight, and optimal schedules across seeds, model families, scales, and stages of pretraining?
Can an online controller update both the graph and mixture while representing negative transfer, saturation, forgetting, and uncertainty?
What gains remain when graph-learning compute and repeated validation are charged to the same end-to-end token/FLOP budget?
Do skill mixtures improve robust downstream capabilities rather than average loss on the same task categories used to define or probe the graph?

competitive_landscape.title: DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining
competitive_landscape.difference: DoReMi uses a proxy/reference-model group-DRO objective to optimize worst-domain excess loss and reports transfer from 280M to 8B without downstream labels. SKILL-IT instead models directed source-to-target skill influence and can condition a dynamic schedule on selected evaluation skills.

competitive_landscape.title: Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance
competitive_landscape.difference: Data Mixing Laws fits explicit mixture-performance functions across sampled mixtures and nests them with model/data scaling laws, selecting a mostly static mixture before large training. SKILL-IT needs directional cross-skill probes but adapts weights from live validation losses.

competitive_landscape.title: RegMix: Data Mixture as Regression for Language Model Pre-training
competitive_landscape.difference: RegMix trains hundreds of ultra-small models on sampled mixtures and regresses unseen-mixture performance, explicitly testing 1M-to-1B and up-to-7B transfer. It searches domain interactions globally but produces a static mixture; SKILL-IT encodes pairwise directed influence and online loss feedback.

competitive_landscape.title: RegMix-D: Dynamic Data Mixing via Proxy Training Trajectories
competitive_landscape.difference: RegMix-D predicts stage-specific mixtures from complete proxy loss trajectories and supports offline schedules or online adaptation, directly challenging SKILL-IT's dynamic-mixing niche. It does not require a human-named prerequisite graph, while SKILL-IT offers an interpretable target-conditioned transfer structure.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first data-driven framework that formalizes LM skills and their ordering, demonstrates nontrivial ordered skill sets, and uses their graph in an online sampler for continual pretraining, fine-tuning, and out-of-domain targets.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Formal definitions, graph-estimation algorithms, mirror-descent derivation, synthetic and Natural Instructions experiments, graph/no-graph and static/online ablations, proxy-to-larger-model transfer, and a 3B RedPajama case support the components of the claim.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The distinctive contribution is target-conditioned dynamic mixing through an interpretable directed transfer graph, broader than source-level worst-domain reweighting. Later regression and mixing-law methods provide stronger global mixture search and scale tests, and RegMix-D covers dynamic schedules without a fixed prerequisite taxonomy. The remaining novelty is therefore the skill-level causal-transfer framing, not an established best general-purpose data-mixture optimizer.

reviewer_notes: Read all 37 extracted pages, including definitions, derivation, all main experiments, graph-construction costs, per-skill tables, scale transfer, weight trajectories, and graph/static ablations. The current target is arXiv v1. Primary arXiv records for DoReMi, Data Mixing Laws, RegMix, and RegMix-D were checked on 2026-08-23; author-reported results are separated from the end-to-end-compute and effect-size audit.
